edits.old: A performance-cost investigation should compare representative sustained workloads and correlate slow-operation periods with available CPU and throttling signals. This is a synthesis from Atlas's burst warning, baseline-based scaling model, and a practitioner upgrade report; a short burst test cannot establish sustained M10 throughput per dollar. (medium confidence)
edits.new: Atlas documents that M10/M20 use burstable performance infrastructure where cloud providers cap CPU usage after burst periods, causing throttling under heavy load, and provides a System: CPU (Steal) % alert (M10/M20 on AWS) and a Normalized System CPU chart for correlating CPU pressure with periods of interest. A performance-cost investigation should therefore correlate slow-operation periods with these CPU signals (this recommendation is a synthesis, not a MongoDB statement). Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/manage-clusters/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/system-cpu-usage/

evidence.quote: Cloud providers cap CPU usage after burst periods, which can cause throttling under heavy load.

Atlas triggers this alert only for AWS EC2 instances that support [AWS burstable instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/burstable-performance-instances.html). Currently, these are `M10` and `M20` cluster types.
View the Normalized System CPU chart to monitor CPU usage of all processes on the node, scaled to a range of 0-100% by dividing by the number of CPU cores.

statements.statement: M10/M20 burstable infrastructure can throttle CPU under heavy load, and Atlas exposes CPU Steal alerts and Normalized System CPU chart to correlate with slow periods.

edits.rationale: The manage-clusters page says M10/M20 support development environments and production environments with low-traffic applications. The manage-clusters page explicitly allows low-traffic production, so the 'scope, not prohibit' point holds.
